Predictive Modeling with Linear Regression Project: ReCell

 

Problem Statement

 

Business Context

 
Buying and selling used phones and tablets used to be something that happened on a handful of online marketplace sites. But the used and refurbished device market has grown considerably over the past decade, and a new IDC (International Data Corporation) forecast predicts that the used phone market would be worth \$52.7bn by 2023 with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 13.6% from 2018 to 2023. This growth can be attributed to an uptick in demand for used phones and tablets that offer considerable savings compared with new models.

Refurbished and used devices continue to provide cost-effective alternatives to both consumers and businesses that are looking to save money when purchasing one. There are plenty of other benefits associated with the used device market. Used and refurbished devices can be sold with warranties and can also be insured with proof of purchase. Third-party vendors/platforms, such as Verizon, Amazon, etc., provide attractive offers to customers for refurbished devices. Maximizing the longevity of devices through second-hand trade also reduces their environmental impact and helps in recycling and reducing waste. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak may further boost this segment as consumers cut back on discretionary spending and buy phones and tablets only for immediate needs.
 

Objective

 
The rising potential of this comparatively under-the-radar market fuels the need for an ML-based solution to develop a dynamic pricing strategy for used and refurbished devices. ReCell, a startup aiming to tap the potential in this market, has hired you as a data scientist. They want you to analyze the data provided and build a linear regression model to predict the price of a used phone/tablet and identify factors that significantly influence it.
 

Data Description

 
The data contains the different attributes of used/refurbished phones and tablets. The data was collected in the year 2021. The detailed data dictionary is given below.


- brand_name: Name of manufacturing brand
- os: OS on which the device runs
- screen_size: Size of the screen in cm
- 4g: Whether 4G is available or not
- 5g: Whether 5G is available or not
- main_camera_mp: Resolution of the rear camera in megapixels
- selfie_camera_mp: Resolution of the front camera in megapixels
- int_memory: Amount of internal memory (ROM) in GB
- ram: Amount of RAM in GB
- battery: Energy capacity of the device battery in mAh
- weight: Weight of the device in grams
- release_year: Year when the device model was released
- days_used: Number of days the used/refurbished device has been used
- normalized_new_price: Normalized price of a new device of the same model in euros
- normalized_used_price: Normalized price of the used/refurbished device in euros

6. A lot of devices nowadays offer great selfie cameras, allowing us to capture our favorite moments with loved ones. What is the distribution of devices offering greater than 8MP selfie cameras across brands?
7. Which attributes are highly correlated with the normalized price of a used device?

# Function to examine the distribution of a numerical feature using combined boxplot and histogram

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """

    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )
# creating the 2 subplots
    # Boxplot
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="blue"
    )

    # Histogram
    if bins:
        sns.histplot(data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins)
    else:
        sns.histplot(data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2)

    # Mean line
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="red", linestyle="--", label="Mean"
    )

    # Median line
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="green", linestyle="-", label="Median"
    )

    ax_hist2.legend()
    ax_hist2.set_title(f"Distribution of {feature}")
In [16]:
# Function to create labeled bar plots with counts or percentages

def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with count or percentage labels

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default None → display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # Total number of observations
    count = data[feature].nunique()  # Number of unique categories

    # Set figure size
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 2, 6))
        order = data[feature].value_counts().index
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 2, 6))
        order = data[feature].value_counts().index[:n]

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=12)

    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        order=order
    )

    # Add labels on top of bars
    for p in ax.patches:
        height = p.get_height()

        if perc:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(100 * height / total)
        else:
            label = int(height)

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2, height),
            ha="center",
            va="bottom",
            size=11,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points"
        )

    plt.title(f"Distribution of {feature}")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Model Performance Check



Let's check the performance of the model using different metrics.

We will be using metric functions defined in sklearn for RMSE, MAE, and R2
.

We will define a function to calculate MAPE and adjusted R2
.

We will create a function which will print out all the above metrics in one go.
In [57]:
# function to compute adjusted R-squared
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]
    k = predictors.shape[1]
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))


# function to compute MAPE
def mape_score(targets, predictions):
    return np.mean(np.abs(targets - predictions) / targets) * 100


# function to compute different metrics to check performance of a regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check regression model performance

    model: regressor
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)  # to compute R-squared
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)  # to compute adjusted R-squared
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))  # to compute RMSE
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAE
    mape = mape_score(target, pred)  # to compute MAPE

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "RMSE": rmse,
            "MAE": mae,
            "R-squared": r2,
            "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
            "MAPE": mape,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

Checking Linear Regression Assumptions

 
- In order to make statistical inferences from a linear regression model, it is important to ensure that the assumptions of linear regression are satisfied.
In [60]:
#Let's define a function to check VIF.

def checking_vif(predictors):
    vif = pd.DataFrame()
    vif["feature"] = predictors.columns

    # calculating VIF for each feature
    vif["VIF"] = [
        variance_inflation_factor(predictors.values, i)
        for i in range(len(predictors.columns))
    ]
    return vif

In [62]:
def treating_multicollinearity(predictors, target, high_vif_columns):
    """
    Checking the effect of dropping the columns showing high multicollinearity
    on model performance (adj. R-squared and RMSE)

    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    high_vif_columns: columns having high VIF
    """
    # empty lists to store adj. R-squared and RMSE values
    adj_r2 = []
    rmse = []

    # build ols models by dropping one of the high VIF columns at a time
    # store the adjusted R-squared and RMSE in the lists defined previously

    for cols in high_vif_columns:

        # defining the new train set
        train = predictors.loc[:, ~predictors.columns.str.startswith(cols)]

        # create the model
        olsmodel = sm.OLS(target, train).fit()

        # adding adj. R-squared and RMSE to the lists
        adj_r2.append(olsmodel.rsquared_adj)
        rmse.append(np.sqrt(olsmodel.mse_resid))

    # creating a dataframe for the results
    temp = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "col": high_vif_columns,
            "Adj. R-squared after_dropping col": adj_r2,
            "RMSE after dropping col": rmse,
        }
    ).sort_values(by="Adj. R-squared after_dropping col", ascending=False)
    temp.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)

    return temp

# initial list of columns
predictors = x_train2.copy()   # use the correct training dataset
cols = predictors.columns.tolist()

# setting an initial max p-value
max_p_value = 1

while len(cols) > 0:

    # defining the train set
    x_train_aux = predictors[cols]

    # add constant (important for OLS)
    x_train_aux_const = sm.add_constant(x_train_aux)

    # fitting the model
    model = sm.OLS(y_train, x_train_aux_const).fit()

    # getting the p-values (excluding constant)
    p_values = model.pvalues.iloc[1:]
    max_p_value = max(p_values)

    # name of the variable with maximum p-value
    feature_with_p_max = p_values.idxmax()

    if max_p_value > 0.05:
        cols.remove(feature_with_p_max)
    else:
        break

selected_features = cols

This Fitted vs Residual plot shows how the residuals (differences between actual and predicted values) behave across the predicted values:

Key Observations:



1. Centered Around Zero:
Most residuals are scattered closely around the horizontal line at 0, indicating that the model’s predictions are generally unbiased.

2. No Clear Pattern:
The residuals are fairly randomly distributed across the range of fitted values, which suggests that the assumption of linearity is reasonably met.

3. Homoscedasticity:
The spread of residuals is roughly consistent across fitted values, meaning there is no strong pattern of increasing or decreasing variance (no clear funnel shape). This indicates the variance of errors is stable, which is good for regression.

4. Outliers:
A few points lie further away from 0, indicating some outliers where the model under- or over-predicted, but they are relatively few.

Overall:
The plot suggests that the model is a good fit for the data, with residuals fairly random and centered around zero, supporting the assumptions of linear regression.
 
TEST FOR NORMALITY
In [72]:
sns.histplot(data=df_pred, x='Residuals')
plt.title("Normality of residuals")
plt.show()
 
Observation:

The histogram of residuals shows a roughly symmetrical, unimodal distribution centered near zero, with only slight left skew and a few outliers. While this suggests approximate normality, formal tests such as the Shapiro-Wilk or Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, along with a Q-Q plot, should be used to confirm. Ensuring normality of residuals is important in linear regression to validate p-values and the accuracy of confidence and prediction intervals. Overall, the residuals appear reasonably normal for model assumptions.

The Q-Q plot shows a subtle S-shape, indicating that the residuals have heavy tails—more extreme values than expected under a normal distribution. The center of the plot aligns well with the reference line, so most residuals behave normally, but the left and right tails deviate, showing unusually small and large values. This suggests the presence of outliers, which could affect statistical tests that assume normality.

TEST FOR HOMOSCEDASTICITY

We will test for homoscedasticity by using the goldfeldquandt test.

If we get a p-value greater than 0.05, we can say that the residuals are homoscedastic. Otherwise, they are heteroscedastic.

Final OLS Regression Model

The regression predicts normalized used price using 11 predictors. The model shows a strong fit:

R-squared = 0.845 and Adjusted R-squared = 0.844, meaning about 84–85% of the variance in used prices is explained by the predictors.

The F-statistic = 1188 (p < 0.001) indicates that the model is statistically significant overall.

Key Predictors:

Positive impact on price: screen_size, main_camera_mp, selfie_camera_mp, weight, normalized_new_price, brand_name_Xiaomi, 4g_yes.

Negative impact on price: battery (slightly), years_since_release, brand_name_Celkon, os_Others.

All coefficients are statistically significant (p < 0.05).

Residual Diagnostics:

Homoscedasticity: Goldfeld-Quandt test p-value = 0.88 → residuals have stable variance.

Normality: Q-Q plot shows a slight S-shape → residuals mostly normal but with heavy tails/outliers.

Fitted vs Residual Plot: Residuals are centered around zero with no obvious pattern, supporting linearity.

Other Notes:

Durbin-Watson ≈ 2.0 → no autocorrelation in residuals.

Skew = -0.562, Kurtosis = 5.574 → residuals have mild left skew and heavier tails than normal.

Condition number = 3.89e4 → potential multicollinearity; consider reviewing correlated predictors.

Conclusion:
The model is a good fit and meets most regression assumptions. Slight deviations from normality (heavy tails) and possible multicollinearity should be noted but are unlikely to invalidate the overall results.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations

 

Actionable Insights



1. Key Drivers of Used Price:

* Positive contributors: Higher screen_size, better main_camera_mp and selfie_camera_mp, higher normalized_new_price, weight, presence of 4G, and the Xiaomi brand all significantly increase used price.
* Negative contributors: Older phones (years_since_release), Celkon brand, os_Others, and higher battery (slightly negative) decrease used price.

2. Brand Influence:

* Xiaomi devices tend to retain value better, while Celkon and non-standard OS devices lose value faster.
* Brand positioning and perceived quality strongly affect resale value.

3. Feature Importance:

* Features like screen size, camera specifications, and original price have the largest impact, suggesting buyers prioritize performance and perceived value over minor physical attributes like weight.

4. Market Trends:

* The negative coefficient for years_since_release reinforces the expected depreciation over time, highlighting that newer devices command higher resale value.

Recommendations



1. Pricing Strategy:

* When pricing used devices, emphasize models with high-performing cameras, larger screens, and popular brands like Xiaomi for premium resale pricing.
* Older devices or less popular brands should be priced lower to reflect expected depreciation and lower market demand.

2. Inventory and Marketing:

* Focus marketing and resale efforts on high-value features (camera quality, screen size, connectivity) to attract buyers willing to pay more.
* Consider segmenting inventory based on brand and age to optimize pricing and promotions.

3. Product Development Guidance (if applicable):

* For manufacturers, investing in camera quality and display improvements can boost resale value, which may influence customer satisfaction and brand loyalty.
* Avoid neglecting software and OS support, as non-standard OS devices tend to lose value faster.

4. Risk Management:

* Outliers in residuals suggest some devices may be over- or under-valued; careful inspection of unusual cases can prevent pricing errors.
* Monitor for multicollinearity among features (e.g., camera and screen size) when adding new predictors to avoid inflated variance in estimates.
